SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI

Van Bach Nguyen Affiliation:  University of Marburg    Qianli Wang Affiliation:  Technische Universität Berlin Affiliation:  German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)    Nils Feldhus Affiliation:  University of Groningen Affiliation:  German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)    Jörg Schlötterer Affiliation:  University of Marburg    Christin Seifert Affiliation:  University of Marburg
Abstract

Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. These pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high response-to-tool faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turns. Overall, SimXAI improves conversational interaction while leaving the underlying XAI resources unchanged11 1 The source code (including evaluation suite) is available at: https://github.com/bach-mr/SimXAI.

22footnotetext: Work done at TU Berlin.

1 Introduction

The XAI community has reached a consensus that explanations should take a conversational form Miller (2019); Lakkaraju et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2025). Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents therefore move beyond one-off explanations and embrace conversational approaches to provide explanations. These conversational explanations have been demonstrated to be more effective for users’ model understanding Shen et al. (2023); Mindlin et al. (2024); He et al. (2025). Conceptually, a ConvXAI agent can be decomposed into two parts: (i) a conversational layer (ConvXAI layer), responsible for managing the interaction with the user, and (ii) the underlying XAI resources, which store or generate the explanatory information (e.g., model/data cards Mitchell et al. (2019); Pushkarna et al. (2022), or feature-attribution methods like SHAP Lundberg and Lee (2017) or counterfactual explanations Mothilal et al. (2020); Ross et al. (2021)). Most current ConvXAI agents (i.a., Nguyen et al. 2023; Slack et al. 2023; Feldhus et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024a) adopt the traditional GUS (Genial Understanding System) architecture Bobrow et al. (1977) for the ConvXAI layer, which comprises three distinct components: natural language understanding (NLU) for intent recognition, dialogue management for context maintenance and rule application, and natural language generation (NLG) for response production. Although such GUS-based ConvXAI layers present explanations through interactive dialogue, they rely on multiple models separately fine-tuned on handcrafted data for intent recognition in NLU, rule-based dialogue management, and template-based response generation in NLG (Figure 1). As a result, they remain limited in contextualization, scalability, and generalization Rastogi et al. (2020). These limitations highlight the need for lightweight, adaptive, and flexible ConvXAI layers. Recent developments suggest that LLMs can fulfill this role and replace traditional ConvXAI layers in such systems Li et al. (2024).

We introduce SimXAI, a simple, lightweight, LLM-centric framework that acts as a ConvXAI layer between users and existing XAI resources (see Figure 1). Unlike rule- or template-based systems, SimXAI uses an LLM to support natural, context-aware dialogue without requiring handcrafted intent datasets or conversational fine-tuning. The layer is data- and model-agnostic. Integrating it into an agent requires only function implementations that provide access to the agent’s existing XAI resources. SimXAI can therefore replace the conversational components of GUS-based agents (e.g., Slack et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2023) while preserving the underlying explanations. SimXAI is not a standalone agent and does not itself select or validate XAI methods. Instead, it provides a modular interface to resources supplied by the host system.

Using LLMs for tool calling is not technically novel. Our contribution is a ConvXAI-specific design that separates a replaceable conversational layer from XAI resources. The design also provides a function interface based on XAI question types and an evaluation framework that separately measures function parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextualization.

Prior work on evaluating ConvXAI has mainly focused on isolated turns Malandri et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2024a) and has often overlooked dialogue context. To address this gap, we evaluate SimXAI on parsing accuracy in single- and multi-turn dialogues, contextualization, and response-to-tool faithfulness. For each aspect, we provide a dataset with manually annotated ground truth, corresponding metrics, and an automated evaluation pipeline. The faithfulness evaluation measures whether the conversational layer preserves the returned XAI output. It does not measure whether the underlying explanation method is faithful to the predictive model.

In a user study with 30 participants, replacing the ConvXAI layer of TalkToModel with SimXAI while keeping the underlying XAI resources unchanged, significantly improved both, perceived interaction quality and task performance.

In summary, our contributions are threefold. First, based on the analysis of limitations of prior work (§2), we introduce SimXAI, an LLM-centric framework that addresses these limitations and offers a practical alternative to conventional ConvXAI layers (§3). Second, we present a multi-aspect evaluation suite for ConvXAI layers, including automated assessment of parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextualization (§4). Third, we show through quantitative evaluation and a user study that replacing a conventional conversational layer with SimXAI improves significantly conversational quality while preserving faithfulness to underlying XAI outputs (§5, §6).

2 Limitations of Conversational Layers in Prior ConvXAI Agents

GUS-based ConvXAI layers (such as Nguyen et al. 2023; Slack et al. 2023; Feldhus et al. 2023) support follow-up questions, but their conversational behavior is typically implemented through task-specific grammars, intent schemas, templates, or dialogue rules. As summarized in Table 1, this design leads to a recurring trade-off between faithfulness and three other dimensions: contextualization, scalability, and generalization.

First, prior systems provide only weak-to-moderate contextualization, handling context primarily through pre-defined operational structures rather than flexible discourse-level reasoning. TalkToModel resolves follow-up questions through grammar operators such as previous_filter and previous_operation Slack et al. (2023). InterroLang extends this design with intent recognition, slot filling, reference resolution, and clarification strategies Feldhus et al. (2023). XAgent supports multi-turn interaction through a fixed dialogue manager and a curated phrase bank Nguyen et al. (2023). Such mechanisms can handle follow-up questions only to a limited extent and often struggle when users rely on ellipsis, anaphora, or long-range dependencies (see Figure 1 for an example of a failure case).

Second, this design leads to low-to-moderate scalability and limited generalization across domains and tasks. TalkToModel requires dataset-specific grammars and synthetic utterance–parse pairs Slack et al. (2023), InterroLang depends on annotated intents, slots, and task-specific operations Feldhus et al. (2023), and XAgent relies on manually curated phrases and response templates Nguyen et al. (2023). As a result, extending such systems to new settings usually requires additional annotation or rule engineering rather than simply integrating new XAI resources. This also limits generalization: prior systems are typically demonstrated in narrow settings, such as tabular data or NLP-specific pipelines, and their conversational control logic does not transfer easily beyond those conditions.

At the same time, these constrained designs maximally preserve faithfulness in response generation. As they generate outputs through rules or templates, the conversational layer is less likely to introduce unsupported claims or misrepresent the underlying XAI method results. The problem with prior systems is not faithfulness itself, but the rigid control logic they use to maintain it. That logic limits how well prior systems handle context and makes these systems hard to adapt across domains.

In contrast, SimXAI addresses these problems by replacing handcrafted conversational control logic with a tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources, without requiring finetuning, handcrafted data, or templates. This design enables strong contextualization, high scalability and high generalization, as it does not rely on domain-specific implementations.

3 SimXAI

SimXAI adds a conversational interface to existing XAI resources using only two components: (1) an off-the-shelf LLM with tool-calling support and (2) a set of general function specifications that map user requests onto available XAI resources. The novelty lies in this ConvXAI-specific separation and interface, rather than in the general mechanism of LLM tool calling. Unlike prior systems, SimXAI does not rely on task-specific grammars, intent schemas, dialogue managers, or response templates. Instead, SimXAI interprets the current user query together with the dialogue history, selects the appropriate function, fills its arguments from context when applicable, and verbalizes the returned result. The backend remains responsible for computing the prediction, explanation, or data/model information returned by that function.

Formally, given a user query qq, dialogue history HH, and a set of available functions 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the system either answers directly or invokes a function t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}. When a function call is required, the system extracts the necessary arguments from qq and HH, asks for clarification if required information cannot be recovered from the dialogue context, executes the function, and generates a final response grounded in the returned output. This design replaces handcrafted conversational control logic with a single tool-calling LLM interface that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Algorithm 1 summarizes this interaction loop.

3.1 Tool-Calling LLM

We use ToolACE-2.5-Llama-3.1-8B22 2 https://huggingface.co/Team-ACE/ToolACE-2.5-Llama-3.1-8B, an off-the-shelf LLM trained for tool-use reasoning Liu et al. (2025); Grattafiori et al. (2024). In SimXAI, the LLM is responsible for four decisions: (i) whether tool use is needed, (ii) if so, which function to call, (iii) how to ground its arguments in the current turn and dialogue history, and (iv) how to generate a final natural-language response from the function output. No additional parser, dialogue manager, or template bank is required.

3.2 Function Set

Our set of functions is based on the question bank of Liao and Varshney (2022); Liao et al. (2020). This question bank was created from practitioner interviews and organized around model-, data-, and context-related questions about AI systems. From this bank, we implement 11 functions: one retrieves the model prediction for a given instance and the other ten address explanatory questions, such as why the model made a particular prediction or how to modify an instance to change the prediction. For each function, we specify its purpose, inputs, arguments, and outputs. Table 2 summarizes the full set. The set is extensible: if no predefined function matches a user’s intent, a new function can be added with its own specification (Figure 2).

Function Specification.

Function specification is critical for ensuring that the LLM calls the correct function. For each function, we adopt a standard specification template (Figure 2) that defines the function name, argument list and types, documentation, and expected input and output types. These specifications are not tied to any particular dataset or model. Instead, we use general specifications that apply across datasets and models, enabling broad generalization (cf. Figure 5 in the appendix for a concrete example of a counterfactual function specification).

4 Evaluation

We evaluate ConvXAI layers along three aspects: parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextualization. Parsing measures whether the system selects the correct function and arguments for a user request, response-to-tool faithfulness measures whether the final response is supported by the returned XAI output, and contextualization measures whether the system uses dialogue history appropriately when interpreting the current turn. Table 4 summarizes the evaluation suite. This scope evaluates the conversational layer only: it neither measures nor guarantees the intrinsic correctness or model-faithfulness of the backend XAI method that produced the tool output. We use this suite for two purposes. First, we assess SimXAI directly across settings of increasing conversational complexity. Second, we qualitatively analyze gains from replacing the conversational components of prior GUS-based ConvXAI systems with SimXAI while keeping their underlying XAI resources unchanged.

4.1 Parsing

Parsing evaluates whether the system maps a user request to the correct function and arguments. We report exact-match accuracy over the selected function. Unlike prior work, which mainly evaluates parsing in single-turn settings Slack et al. (2023); Feldhus et al. (2023); Nguyen et al. (2023), we consider three levels of conversational complexity.

Single-turn parsing.

We evaluate standard single-turn function selection on two datasets in ConvXAI settings: CoXQL Wang et al. (2024b) for explanation request parsing (Figure 4) and Compass Wang et al. (2025) for user input extraction (Figure 6). In this setting, the current query can be interpreted without dialogue history.

Multi-turn parsing.

To evaluate short-range contextual parsing, we construct Compass-MultiTurn from Compass by merging related single-turn interactions into short conversations and removing redundant user turns (details in Appendix A). In this setting, the use of recent dialogue history is required to parse the users’ intent correctly.

Dialogue-level parsing.

To evaluate long-range dependencies, we generate synthetic dialogue-level datasets in two domains: sentiment analysis SYN-Sentiment and heart rate prediction SYN-HeartRate. Each of the two datasets combines dialogues generated under two settings: Constrained, in which we provide our 11 function specifications in the prompt and ask GPT-5.1 to generate realistic conversations covering all operations, and Unconstrained, in which GPT-5.1 is prompted to generate realistic conversations without any predefined constraints. Each user turn defines one parsing instance, with the full preceding dialogue provided as context. Human validation assessed these synthetic dialogues as mostly realistic (details in Appendix B).

Together, these datasets assess whether ConvXAI systems can select the correct function corresponding to user’s intent. They range from isolated questions up to full multi-turn conversations with long range dependencies. Table 3 summarizes the parsing datasets.

4.2 Response-to-Tool Faithfulness

As LLMs are prone to hallucination Huang et al. (2025), we evaluate the faithfulness of the agent’s responses with respect to the provided XAI resources. Following prior work Adlakha et al. (2024), we define response-to-tool faithfulness as the extent to which the conversational layer preserves the information contained in a returned XAI output without introducing unsupported claims. This is distinct from the intrinsic faithfulness of the XAI method to the predictive model, which is outside our scope.

We construct two faithfulness datasets, SYN-QA-Sentiment and SYN-QA-HeartRate, based on SYN-Sentiment and SYN-HeartRate. The datasets contain 71 question–answer pairs covering prediction lookup, explanation outputs, model descriptions, and dataset information. For each question, we manually construct a gold standard function output and evaluate whether the system response faithfully preserves this information using a binary judgment and accuracy as aggregated metric.

4.3 Contextualization

Contextualization evaluates whether the system uses dialogue history appropriately to answer the current query. We first assess context relevance by manually determining whether a query can be answered independently or requires the preceding dialogue. For queries that depend on prior context, we then assess whether the response incorporates the necessary dialogue history to resolve the current turn coherently. This contextual answer coherence is a binary judgment, aggregated as accuracy (the fraction of contextually coherent answers).

5 Results

To assess SimXAI, we report performance on parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextual coherence. Following recent work on LLM-based evaluation Xu et al. (2025); Tamber et al. (2025), we additionally examine opportunities for automated evaluation by measuring the agreement between human rating and LLM-as-a-judge.33 3 We use https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Specifically, we report how often the LLM judge assigns the same label as the human annotator for response-to-tool faithfulness and contextualization, including context relevance and contextual coherence.

5.1 SimXAI Performance

Table 4 reports results across the three aspects in the evaluation suite: parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextualization.

For parsing, SimXAI performs strongly in all settings, achieving above 86% accuracy for single-turn, multi-turn, and dialogue-level evaluation. Interestingly, accuracy is higher on the multi-turn and dialogue-level datasets, suggesting that dialogue context helps the model to resolve user intents better.

In most cases (over 91%), SimXAI produces responses that are faithful to the tool output, indicating that the conversational layer preserves the returned XAI information rather than introducing unsupported claims. This is particularly important because SimXAI replaces rule- and template-based conversational components with an LLM-based interface, which may increase the risk of hallucinations. These results do not evaluate the intrinsic faithfulness of the backend XAI methods.

SimXAI further shows high contextual answer coherence across domains: 90.91% for sentiment analysis and 94.74% for heart rate, indicating that prior dialogue context is generally incorporated correctly in context-dependent queries.

Overall, SimXAI performs well across all three aspects of the evaluation suite. Parsing accuracy remains high from single-turn to dialogue-level evaluation, responses are usually supported by the returned XAI outputs, and most context-dependent queries are answered coherently.

5.2 LLM-as-a-judge Performance

Figure 3 shows the agreement between LLM-as-a-judge and human annotation. The agreement on response-to-tool faithfulness is high (around 90%), suggesting that LLM-based evaluation is a promising proxy for this aspect on our datasets. While the agreement on contextual relevance in sentiment analysis is equally high (around 90%), it drops to 76.60% in heart rate prediction. This indicates that automatically determining whether a query depends on prior context remains challenging in some domains. For contextual answer coherence, the LLM judge agrees with human annotations in more than 80% of cases across both domains, suggesting that it can serve as a useful proxy for coherence evaluation.

In summary, evaluation with LLM-as-a-judge shows potential for automated assessment of response-to-tool faithfulness and contextualization. Despite lower agreement on context relevance in heart rate prediction, it may still serve as an efficient approach for initial comparative evaluation.

6 GUS-based system comparison

SimXAI is designed to be integrated into existing conversational XAI agents by replacing their original conversational components. We qualitatively examine how SimXAI can improve existing systems, by replacing the conversational layer of the ConvXAI agents TalkToModel Slack et al. (2023), InterroLang Feldhus et al. (2023), and XAgent Nguyen et al. (2023) with SimXAI and re-assess cases, in which the original system failed (e.g., due to missing context handling abilities).

For each baseline, we keep the original function set and underlying XAI outputs fixed, and replace only the module that maps user requests and dialogue history onto function selection and response generation. This isolates the contribution of SimXAI acting solely as conversational layer and not as a modified ConvXAI backend.

We further conduct a user study on the integration of SimXAI into TalkToModel, a representative grammar-based system. We directly compare the original model with its SimXAI-integrated counterpart in terms of both, objective and subjective metrics.

6.1 Qualitative results

Figure 1 shows an example failure case of incorrect context handling of TalkToModel’s native conversational layers. TalkToModel fails to maintain contextual understanding because the agent misinterprets the referent of “it” (anaphora), which leads to an incorrect final decision. Replacing TalkToModel’s conversational layers by SimXAI fixes this issue and correctly resolves the context in the same conversation dialogue. We observe similar patterns of incorrect context handling in the other agents under comparison, which are partially unable to provide an answer at all. Replacing the conversational layers of these agents by SimXAI corrects such issues (examples in Appendix C).

6.2 User Study

We conduct a controlled within-subjects study to evaluate whether integrating SimXAI into TalkToModel Slack et al. (2023) 1) improves the perceived quality of the conversation and 2) leads to a better understanding of the machine learning model. To isolate the effect of the conversational component, we keep all other components (datasets, classifiers, and XAI resources) unchanged. We compare two agents: (i) the original TalkToModel with its fine-tuned ConvXAI layers and (ii) TalkToModel with SimXAI replacing the ConvXAI layers. Both agents follow the original TalkToModel configuration described by Slack et al. (2023).

6.2.1 Setup

We recruited 30 lay participants via Prolific.44 4 https://www.prolific.com/ Participants receive a compensation of $8/hour This sample size aligns with prior HCI and XAI studies evaluating interactive explanation systems Kaur et al. (2020); Slack et al. (2023). Participants interact with both agents using the Diabetes dataset Kahn (1994), as in the original TalkToModel study.

For each agent, participants complete three tasks. These tasks cover multiple categories from an established XAI question taxonomyLiao et al. (2020), including data understanding, local explanations, and counterfactual inspection. Each task contains at least two questions, for a total of nine questions across all tasks. The questions are sampled from a pool of predefined multiple-choice questions for each task (details in Appendix Section D.1). They are designed to be answerable using the ground-truth information provided by the agent’s explanations. Some questions by design require multi-turn interactions to arrive at the correct answer, in order to assess conversational coherence and context handling. We randomize the order of agents, and although the question types remain consistent across conditions, specific values (e.g., instance identifiers) are varied to mitigate learning effects.

We collect both, objective and subjective measures. Objective metrics are (1) answer accuracy, (2) conversational efficiency measured as the number of turns per correctly answered question, which is commonly used in dialogue agent evaluation Su et al. (2016); Peng et al. (2017), and (3) indicators of conversational breakdowns, such as repeated or rephrased questions and agent failures, where the agent does not provide meaningful answers. Subjective measures consist of two parts. First, we use the 5-point Likert BUS-11 usability scale Borsci and Schmettow (2024), which includes 11 items across five subscales, focusing on perceived conversation and information quality and perceived chatbot functionality. Second, we include a pairwise comparison questionnaire between the two agents to assess user preference and explanation effectiveness.

6.2.2 Results

This section summarizes the key objective and subjective results. Details on the significance tests for the reported metrics, the full BUS-11 scale, and the complete pairwise comparison are provided in Appendix Section D.3.

Objective results.

Replacing TalkToModel’s conversational component with SimXAI leads to clear improvements in both, task performance and perceived interaction quality. Table 5 shows that participants achieve substantially higher accuracy with SimXAI than with the original TalkToModel (92.1% vs. 59.0%, p<.001p<.001). SimXAI also reduces interaction costs: users complete the task in fewer turns on average (10.0 vs. 12.4 turns) and in less time (5.8 vs. 7.4 minutes). Across all sessions, this translates to roughly half as many turns per correct answer with SimXAI (1.32 vs. 2.70).

Subjective results.

Table 6 reports the BUS-11 usability ratings. We observe the largest improvements in clarity of communication, context tracking, helpfulness in achieving the user’s goal, and providing an appropriate amount of information (all p<.001p<.001). Perceived response time is the only item where SimXAI scores lower, suggesting a possible trade-off between conversational quality and latency. We attribute this to the models deployed for parsing in TalkToModel, which are comparably smaller (ranging from 60M to 6B) than to the tool-augmented LLM we use in SimXAI (§3.1). However, the difference is not statistically significant (p>0.1).

Pairwise comparison.

80.0% of the participants prefer SimXAI overall, while 16.7% prefer TalkToModel and 3.3% indicate no preference (cf. Table 9 in the Appendix). We observe the same proportions for perceived task effectiveness.

Overall, the user study shows that replacing the conversational component of TalkToModel with SimXAI improves both, perceived interaction quality and task performance, even when the underlying XAI resources remain unchanged.

7 Related Work

Besides the systems analyzed in §2, that rely on fine-tuned models, off-the-shelf LLMs are increasingly adopted in ConvXAI. Nguyen et al. (2024) extend XAgent by Llama-2 Touvron et al. (2023) for postprocessing NLG and answering general factual questions (e.g., about machine learning terminology). KnowThySelf Prasai et al. (2025) is a multi-agent framework, which at its core still resembles the GUS architecture. It employs Gemma3-27B Team et al. (2025) for most parts of NLU and NLG, while user intents are matched to specialized agents by embedding-based similarity, using nomic-embed-text Nussbaum et al. (2025). These specialized agents encapsulate XAI resources. Closest to our work is Echo Vanbrabant et al. (2025), another agentic framework with a tool-calling LLM at its core. However, Echo trades faithfulness for human validation “… might not always result in a helpful or correct answer […] This further highlights the importance of human-in-the-loop workflows, in which the LLM can try again until the answer is satisfactory”. This undermines the purpose of ConvXAI to explain a model’s true reasoning, as any plausible answer is likely satisfactory. Yet, plausibility and correctness are different evaluation criteria that should not be conflated Nauta et al. (2023) (a plausible answer might not be correct, while a correct one might not be plausible, e.g., if the model’s reasoning is flawed).

All these systems are demos without quantitative or qualitative evaluation. Unlike prior GUS-based systems or existing tool-calling ConvXAI agents, our contribution is not the generic tool-calling mechanism itself. SimXAI introduces a simple, lightweight, open-source intermediate layer with a ConvXAI-specific separation between conversational control and underlying XAI resources, an extensible XAI function design, and a dedicated evaluation suite. The measured faithfulness in this suite is response-to-tool faithfulness and should not be interpreted as validation of the backend explanation method.

8 Conclusion

SimXAI enables natural conversational interactions with existing XAI resources through general callable functions. Across evaluations of parsing, response-to-tool faithfulness, and contextualization, its lightweight LLM-centric design supports conversational explanations while usually preserving the information returned by the XAI resources. Our user study shows that replacing the conversational layers of a traditional GUS-based ConvXAI agent by SimXAI significantly improves task performance and perceived interaction quality. This suggests that LLM-centric architectures provide tangible benefits to users in understanding AI model behavior. In future work, we plan to explore and enhance fully automated evaluation for LLM-based conversational XAI layers. Based on that, we plan to study how LLM choice affects tool calling and to develop further improvements to ConvXAI.

Limitations

Like other LLM-based systems, SimXAI introduces additional latency and remains susceptible to hallucinations.

SimXAI improves only the conversational component: it assumes that appropriate XAI resources are already available and does not assess the intrinsic quality, correctness, or model-faithfulness of the underlying explanation methods themselves. Consequently, a response can be faithful to a tool output even when that output is incomplete or misleading.

We do not study the impact of the LLM choice for tool calling or LLM-as-a-judge. Our experiments use a lightweight 8B LLaMA 3.1 model, and results may vary with other models.

Appendix A Parsing

Failure in single-turn parsing.

Figure 6 shows the comparison between single-turn and multi-turn parsing. For multi-turn parsing, LLMs should be able to utilize the context from previous turns. As illustrated in the third example in Figure 6, users can simply use pronouns like “it” to reference previous questions without repeating the actual question from the last turn. Such cases would fail in single-turn parsing, as there is no conversational context to resolve what “it” refers to.

From single-turn to multi-turn.

Table 3 To build the multi-turn version (Figure 6, right side), related consecutive questions that operated on the same input text were grouped together into multi-turn conversation sets. Specifically, questions that originally repeated the full instance text had those explicit instance references replaced with pronouns like “it” turning them into natural follow-up turns. This way, the conversation flows naturally: the first turn establishes the target text, and subsequent turns refer back to it implicitly — just as a human would in real dialogue. In total, we created 10 multi-turn dialogues with averaging 4–6 turns each.

Appendix B Realism Validation

Because the conversations in our dataset were generated using GPT-5.1, we additionally evaluated their realism from a human perspective to verify that they resemble plausible explanatory dialogues.

Specifically, we asked five members of our research group with a background in machine learning to assess the realism of user utterances in the synthetically generated explanatory conversations. Participants were asked to imagine themselves as users seeking to understand how a classification model makes its decisions. They were then presented with generated dialogues between a User and an Explainer. Their task was to judge whether the User’s messages resembled authentic user questions, reflected a consistent level of knowledge, and remained on topic throughout the conversation.

For each conversation, participants provided a rating on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (completely unrealistic) to 5 (completely realistic). In addition to the numerical rating, respondents were required to provide a justification for their score, allowing us to collect both quantitative assessments and qualitative rationales regarding perceived conversational realism.

The average score across all conversations was 3.75, suggesting that the generated dialogues achieved a reasonable level of perceived realism.

Appendix C Qualitative examples

In this section, we present additional qualitative results illustrating cases where the original conversational XAI agents fail to capture dialogue context and how SimXAI improves their responses. Table 7 provides examples for each existing agent. Each agent operates on different tasks and exhibits different types of contextualization failures. SimXAI improves these responses across all cases without requiring task-specific or architecture-specific adaptations.

Appendix D User Study Details

D.1 Question Pool

Table 8 presents the three tasks and the corresponding question templates that participants were asked to answer. The questions cover several categories of the XAI question taxonomy Liao et al. (2020), including data understanding, local explanations, and counterfactual inspection.

Some question templates contain placeholders that are replaced with specific values during the study. For these questions, the feature and value are randomly selected when generating the question. The study uses two IDs, which are randomly assigned to the conversational agents.

Each task includes multiple possible questions, and all three tasks are presented to each participant. For each task, questions are randomly selected from the pool without replacement, ensuring that within a single session participants receive as many different questions as possible.

Several selection rules are applied. Bolded questions are always asked, and all types are always included. In addition, italicized questions represent follow-up questions that are always selected when their preceding question appears.

D.2 Instructions and User Interface

Figure 7 shows screenshots of general instructions and informed consent, Figure 8 screenshots of information on the overall study procedure and how to conduct the tasks in the study and Figure 9 shows the interface, participants interact with.

D.3 Results

Across 30 completed sessions, integrating SimXAI into TalkToModel improved both objective task performance and subjective user experience. Unless otherwise noted, we report two-tailed paired tt-tests over participant-level scores. Table 10 summarizes the objective outcomes, Table 11 reports the BUS-11 item means, Table 12 presents the statistical comparisons, and Table 9 summarizes the pairwise preferences.

Objective performance.

As shown in Table 10, SimXAI substantially improves users’ ability to answer explanation-related questions correctly. If we count all cases when users indicated that the question is not answerable (“unable to answer”) as incorrect, accuracy increases from 53.3 ±\pm 19.6 with TalkToModel to 84.1 ±\pm 17.7 with SimXAI. The same pattern holds when excluding unable to answer responses from the denominator, with accuracy increasing from 59.0 ±\pm 21.3 to 92.1 ±\pm 11.6. The corresponding paired tests in Table 12 confirm that both improvements are highly significant (p<.001p<.001 in both cases).

The aggregate counts in Table 10 show the same trend: participants produced many more correct answers with SimXAI (227) than with TalkToModel (138). Importantly, both systems generated the same number of explicit unable to answer responses (24 each), suggesting that the gain came primarily from better answers rather than fewer abstentions.

SimXAI also made interactions more efficient. Compared with TalkToModel, it reduced average chat time (7.4 ±\pm 3.3 minutes vs. 5.8 ±\pm 3.0 minutes) and average conversation length (12.4 ±\pm 4.1 turns vs. 10.0 ±\pm 1.8 turns). This pattern is also reflected in the turns-per-correct-answer measure reported in Table 10, which was notably lower for SimXAI (1.32) than for TalkToModel (2.70). Overall, users reached correct answers more quickly and with fewer conversational steps.

Subjective evaluation.

The subjective ratings mirror the objective results. Table 11 shows that SimXAI received higher mean ratings on 10 of the 11 BUS-11 items, and Table 12 shows that 9 of these differences are statistically significant. The strongest improvements are observed on dimensions central to multi-turn explanatory dialogue, especially clarity, context retention, helpfulness, and informativeness. For example, users rate SimXAI higher for clear communication (4.60 vs. 3.33), keeping track of conversational context (4.37 vs. 3.13), and helping them achieve their goal (4.37 vs. 3.10).

The same overall trend holds across the remaining items: SimXAI is rated as easier to understand, more accurate, and easier to use for finding information. Only two BUS-11 items do not differ significantly. First, privacy communication is rated relatively low in both conditions, indicating that neither system communicated privacy-related issues particularly well. Second, perceived waiting/response time slightly favors TalkToModel numerically, but the difference is not significant. Taken together, the BUS-11 results show that SimXAI mainly improves the quality and usefulness of the interaction. These aspects are central to ConvXAI.

Pairwise comparison.

The direct comparison results in Table 9 further support this pattern. A large majority of participants prefer SimXAI overall (80.0%), while only 16.7% prefer TalkToModel and 3.3% report no preference. The same distribution appears for perceived task effectiveness: 80.0% judge SimXAI more helpful, 16.7% prefer TalkToModel, and 3.3% consider the two systems equally helpful. These preferences are consistent with both the objective performance results and the BUS-11 ratings.

Summary.

Overall, the results across Tables 10–9 show a consistent pattern: replacing TalkToModel’s conversational component with SimXAI improves answer quality, increases task success, reduces interaction cost, and leads to more favorable user judgments. The clearest gains appear on aspects that matter most for explanation-oriented multi-turn interaction, namely clarity, contextual coherence, helpfulness, and efficiency.
